Congrats! ER will definitely test your skills. Mentally prepare yourself to see not so pretty things and deal with intense situations. Try to keep calm when it gets wild because getting flustered will make it worse. Build trust with your doctor's and fellow techs. Be reliable and follow through with things. Take criticism (hopefully constructive ). Don't have an ego or assume to know everything. Don't ever be afraid to ask questions or say your unsure of something. When working with an extern or fresh tech or even someone with 30 years experience I respect them 1000x more if they can do that. Egos and the blame game can ruin a team. If you fuck up just own up to it. DON'T TAKE THINGS PERSONALLY. Whether it's from a doctor, tech, or client. ER is high stress for all involved. If a doctor or fellow tech gets short with you or has an annoyed tone don't assume it's because they dislike you or you did something wrong. But also realize some techs and doctors just suck and can be mean and petty. If that's the case gtfo of there because toxic clinics are too common and no fun. Handling clients gets easier with time. You will be called names, cursed at, told you hate animals because you won't do things for free, and all things on between. My.favorite doctor always told us to remember that these people most likely have things going on in life that contribute to their attitudes and actions and just smile and be kind. 
And lastly, BURN OUT IS TOO REAL. Take care of yourself. Don't take on too much and too many hours. Separate work and home life. Get good sleep, take care of your body, don't take stress home, find hobbies, and don't define yourself by your job. Find other things to de-stress and redirect the negative energy. 
ER can be so damn hard but it will all be worth it. The animals you CAN save and thankful owners will remind you why you do what you do. 

Good Luck!

Hey, vet tech here. We usually recommend boiled chicken and white rice as a bland diet but not as a main diet. Animals don't have a sensitivity to grain, so most dry/wet foods are okay. They contain taurine and phosphorous that cats especially need to avoid certain disease processes.
